bright-tree.name: Bright Tree
bright-tree.sub: Diamond Valley, Sunshine Coast hinterland Qld · Group 3 · a regenerative R&D property in a forest corridor
bright-tree.sources: Queensland 1 m LiDAR (2022) and cadastre; rainfall from Nambour (040988); LiDAR canopy 2008–2022; the design map.
big: Water is the spine: catch and store high, move it by gravity and pumps (ram or Bunyip), and treat and reuse wastewater through reed beds.
Almost two-thirds of the land is steeper than 50%: the forest is the senior partner, and food goes on the gentler, already-disturbed ground near the house.
Fire tracks on contour at 10% or less double as access and low-fire food gardens, with the goat zones grazing fuel down.
principles: LiDAR canopy history 2008–2022, Land for Wildlife assessment, drone surveys and fixed soil points.
Staged horizons; rainwater first, then pioneers; satellite planting patches.
Tanks high above the house, hand-built weirs and ponds, solar, carbon in regrowth forest.
Whole-property water and fire first, then zones, then beds and species.
Designing for fire and drier springs; successors in mind.
Stage 1 gardens, fruit along the tracks, workshops, consulting and stays.
Wastewater through reed beds to the fruit forest; compost; waste as another's input.
Native nitrogen fixers, grown mulch, local timber, the forest's own regeneration.
The forest edge as the richest design zone; old disturbed ground for food.
Tracks that are firebreaks, access and gardens; goats that graze fuel.
Forest-garden interface, syntropic layers, many people and skills on site.
Measure tanks, erosion and species over time; design notebooks record changes.

bellbunya.name: Bellbunya
bellbunya.sub: Belli Park, Sunshine Coast hinterland Qld · Group 2 · an eco retreat, sustainable community and education centre
bellbunya.sources: Queensland 1 m LiDAR and cadastre; SILO daily climate 1995–2025; the design map.
big: A gentle site by hinterland standards: over half of the 16 ha is under 18% slope, so buildings, gardens and orchards have room.
The dam is the water heart of the property: keep its catchment vegetated and plan overflow paths past the accommodation.
Growth (new cabins, accommodation and a restaurant) should follow the zones: daily-use gardens beside the buildings, orchard and dam surrounds beyond.
principles: Walk the land in each season; map where people actually go before adding paths.
New cabins one at a time, each with its own roof water and garden.
The dam, roof tanks and mulch; solar on the larger roofs.
Zones from the main building out; slope and water first, buildings and plants after.
Fire-wise buildings; plantings chosen for drier, hotter springs.
Seasonal produce for guests (Bellbunya's own 65% to 80% target), workshops and stays.
Compost and worm systems for the kitchen and restaurant; greywater to orchards.
Volunteers and permablitz days; chop-and-drop mulch; bees and birds.
The dam edge and forest margins as productive, habitat-rich edges.
Accommodation that also collects water and frames gardens.
Food forest layers, natives and exotics, many people and skills.
Area stewards and quarterly reviews: change the design as the community learns.

noosa-forest-retreat.name: Noosa Forest Retreat
noosa-forest-retreat.sub: Kin Kin, Noosa hinterland Qld · the PDC host site
noosa-forest-retreat.sources: Queensland 1 m LiDAR and cadastre; SILO daily climate 1995–2025; the design map.
big: Steep forested land: about 40% is steeper than 50%, so most of it stays as forest and the gardens concentrate on the benches around the buildings.
The western mountain and rainforest shade the site from about 2 pm, so the west becomes a moisture-management zone rather than a hot one.
Water stored high and moved by gravity serves the retreat, the gardens and fire protection together.
principles: The PDC itself: students observing the site through the seasons.
Garden beds and orchard grown out from the buildings step by step.
Tanks, dams and ponds; mulch and living soil; solar.
Sun paths and the afternoon shade of the western mountain set the layout.
Fire, drought and wetter wet seasons planned for together.
Food for the retreat, teaching, and stays.
Composting toilets and compost for the gardens.
Rainforest regeneration and native pollinators.
The rainforest edge and creek banks as rich, productive edges.
Buildings, water, teaching and gardens supporting each other.
Rainforest, orchard and garden species side by side.
Each year's PDC group reviews and refines the design.

willow-vale-team.name: Willow Vale
willow-vale-team.sub: Bowman, Mid Coast NSW · Group 4 · the orchard and food forest design
willow-vale-team.sources: NSW 5 m elevation and property register; the group's draft presentation; the design map.
big: The orchard (about 1,500 m²) faces east on a 20% slope: water first, with the tank on the north-west high corner giving 4–7 m of head to a gravity main.
Landslip and creek erosion were observed by the owner: short micro-basins with spillways, not long swales, and a 10–20 m+ buffer to Camp Creek.
Guilds under the mature citrus, espalier rows, keyhole beds and a rotational chicken run build a layered, productive orchard.
principles: The owner's own notes on slips, floods and frost shaped the plan.
Micro-basins instead of big earthworks; trees planted March–May in stages.
Tank on the high corner, IBCs on the shed, a gravity main to the orchard.
Slope, sun and water first; species chosen last.
Species swaps for weeds and low chill; designing for fire from the State Forest.
Citrus, stone fruit, figs, olives and eggs.
Compost bays and chicken run cycling the orchard's waste.
Chickens as weeders and fertilisers; pigeon pea and local wattle for nitrogen.
The creek corridor and woodland as wildlife edges.
Chickens, guilds and espalier rows all working the same ground.
Guilds under the mature citrus; natives and fruit together.
Soil test before planting; adjust after the first season.
